analysis.one_liner: Restores federal Clean Water Act protection to all U.S. waters, including isolated wetlands and streams.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2001 Supreme Court ruling limited which waters federal Clean Water Act rules cover, this bill wrote a broad definition of protected waters directly into the law, covering all interstate and intrastate waters, their tributaries, wetlands, ponds, and intermittent streams. The goal was to restore the full scope of water pollution protections that existed before the ruling. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks water drawn from sources fed by wetlands and small streams, communities that rely on wetlands for flood protection, hunters, anglers, and outdoor businesses that depend on waterfowl and fish habitat. The bill's findings note that millions of people depend on these waters to filter drinking water supplies and that half of America's ducks breed in them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents, hunters, anglers, water drinkers

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the narrower term 'navigable waters' throughout the Clean Water Act with 'waters of the United States', defined to include all interstate and intrastate waters, their tributaries, wetlands, ponds, mudflats, and intermittent streams, restoring the broadest reading of federal pollution-control jurisdiction.

The bill's findings state that millions of people depend on intrastate and isolated wetlands to filter pollutants from runoff and recharge drinking water supplies, and that filling or draining such wetlands causes or worsens flooding that damages homes and businesses.

The findings cite recreational economies built on waterfowl hunting, fishing, and birdwatching that generate billions of dollars a year, all of which depend on habitat in the smaller waters the bill protects.

analysis.who_pays: Real estate developers, home builders, road builders, landfill operators, and resource extraction companies that fill wetlands or discharge into small streams and would have needed federal permits or faced pollution limits on those activities. Landowners who want to build on wetland parcels also bear new permitting costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Developers and industries discharging into small waters

drawbacks.text: The bill gives federal regulators jurisdiction over virtually every pond, ditch-adjacent stream, and wet patch in the country, which means ordinary landowners and small builders could face federal permitting before working on their own property — the very expansion the Supreme Court had ruled exceeded what Congress had written.

The bill's own findings acknowledge that wetlands are routinely filled for roads, housing subdivisions, and commercial buildings, so the protection comes directly at the cost of slowing and raising the price of that construction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is broad and the compliance burden real: extending federal permitting to isolated wetlands and intermittent streams protects drinking water and flood control for millions of people, but also adds regulatory cost and delay for landowners and builders, some of them small operations. The bill preserves state roles in permitting and allows states to adopt stricter standards, which tempers but does not eliminate that cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Oberstar, joined by Dingell, DeFazio, and Borski, introduced the bill on July 24, 2002, in response to the 2001 Supreme Court decision in Solid Waste Agency of Northern Cook County v. Army Corps of Engineers, which held that 'navigable waters' as written did not cover isolated ponds and wetlands based solely on migratory birds.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and two days later to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, and expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The bill carried 28 cosponsors — 27 of 208 House Democrats and the chamber's single Independent — and no Republican cosponsors.

The bill was essentially a legislative response to the SWANCC ruling: its findings section builds the case that isolated and intrastate waters have a substantial effect on interstate commerce, as the basis for congressional authority to regulate them under the Commerce Clause.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers, home builders, landfill and resource-extraction operators, and landowners who fill wetlands or discharge into small streams are better off: the narrower post-SWANCC jurisdiction stayed in place, so those waters remained outside federal Clean Water Act permitting for another two decades of litigation.

for.name: James L. Oberstar
for.role: U.S. Representative, D-MN; lead sponsor and ranking member of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write a broad 'waters of the United States' definition into the Clean Water Act.

for.name: John Dingell, Peter DeFazio, and Robert Borski
for.role: Original cosponsors; senior House Democrats on transportation and environment matters
for.what_they_did: Joined Oberstar in introducing the bill on its first day.

against.name: Don Young
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill went to a subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: Developers and industries that fill or discharge into wetlands and small streams
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the narrower jurisdiction left in place after the SWANCC ruling and had an interest in keeping the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Real estate development and home building
industries.note: The bill would have required federal permits before filling wetlands for subdivisions, roads, and commercial buildings. Its cost is precisely the public's gain in flood protection and water filtration.
Discharges into small streams, ponds, and isolated wetlands would have become federally regulated, tightening pollution limits the narrower reading allowed to lapse.
Solid waste landfills are among the wetland-filling activities the bill's findings single out as subject to federal jurisdiction.

industries.industry: Municipal water systems and groundwater users
industries.note: Wetlands that recharge and filter drinking water supplies would fall back under pollution-control protections, lowering treatment burdens over time.
